title: Java Exceptions Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of Java exception handling: checked vs unchecked, try/catch/finally, try-with-resources, throw vs throws, custom exceptions and the common runtime exceptions.

chapters.title: Exception Mental Model
points: Throwable hierarchy: Throwable splits into Error (JVM failures like OutOfMemoryError, do not catch) and Exception
Checked exceptions extend Exception but not RuntimeException; the compiler forces catch or declare (IOException, SQLException)
Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException (or Error); no compiler enforcement (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException)
Rule of thumb: checked for recoverable conditions the caller can handle, unchecked for programming bugs
Mistake: catching Throwable or Exception broadly swallows Errors and bugs; catch the most specific type

chapters.title: try, catch and finally Flow
points: Syntax: try { risky } catch (IOException e) { handle } finally { cleanup }; try needs at least one catch or finally
Catch blocks are checked top to bottom; first matching type wins, so subclasses must come before superclasses or compile fails
Multi-catch: catch (IOException | SQLException e) handles unrelated types; e is implicitly final and the types cannot be related by inheritance
finally runs whether or not an exception occurs, even after return; it skips only on System.exit() or JVM crash
Mistake: return or throw inside finally overrides the try result and silently discards the original exception

chapters.title: try-with-resources
points: Syntax: try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(f))) { ... } auto-closes any AutoCloseable resource
Resources close in reverse order of declaration, before any catch or finally block runs
If the body and close() both throw, the body exception is primary and the close exception is attached via getSuppressed()
Java 9+ allows an effectively final existing variable: try (res) { ... }
Mistake: using manual finally { close() } instead; it is verbose and a failing close() can hide the original exception

chapters.title: throw vs throws and Custom Exceptions
points: throw is a statement that raises one exception object: throw new IllegalStateException("msg")
throws is a method signature clause declaring checked exceptions the method may pass up: void read() throws IOException
Custom checked exception: class AppException extends Exception; custom unchecked: extends RuntimeException
Provide constructors (message) and (message, cause); wrap lower-level errors: throw new AppException("load failed", e)
Overriding method cannot throw broader checked exceptions than the parent method declares; it may throw fewer or unchecked ones

chapters.title: Common Runtime Exceptions
points: NullPointerException: calling a method or field on a null reference; prevent with null checks, Objects.requireNonNull, Optional
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException / IndexOutOfBoundsException: index < 0 or >= length (valid range 0 to length-1)
ClassCastException: invalid downcast; guard with instanceof before casting
NumberFormatException (subclass of IllegalArgumentException): Integer.parseInt("abc"); ArithmeticException: integer divide by zero (double gives Infinity instead)
ConcurrentModificationException: removing from a collection during a for-each loop; use Iterator.remove() or removeIf

chapters.title: Exceptions Cheat Sheet
points: Hierarchy: Throwable → Error | Exception → RuntimeException (unchecked); everything else under Exception is checked
Order of events: try → matching catch → finally; resources close before catch runs
Keywords: throw raises an object, throws declares in signature, finally always cleans up, try(...) auto-closes
Best practice: catch specific types, never swallow with an empty catch, always preserve the cause when wrapping
Interview Point: Explain checked vs unchecked; does finally run after return; what is suppressed exception; can you override a method with a broader throws clause
